face: Your banner is known in these hills, ser {player}, and not kindly. Turn your horse about before my patience and my spears both run dry.
Ser {player}, I have heard of your sort. They talk loudly at feast tables and run quickly from the field. Step aside.
A fine cloak for a wanderer who has never bled for anything. Keep to the far side of my road and we shall both be spared the trouble.
My house remembers every slight, and the name {player} stands high on our list of grievances. Do not give us reason to add a new line.
Laugh if you like at my warnings, ser {player}. The crows over this valley have eaten better riders than you for lesser insults.
I will not share bread with a sworn enemy of my oath. Ride on, and count yourself fortunate that my blade is still sheathed.
Your ancestors gave their word freely and broke it often, and I see their dishonour still lives in you. Speak quickly, ser {player}, before my temper outruns my courtesy.
The toll on this road is paid in coin or in blood, ser {player}. You have neither to spare, so choose with care.
Some wanderers are remembered only by the graves they dig. I will see that yours is marked well, ser {player}.
Weary I am of rivals who hide behind fine words. Show me your face and your intent, or I shall take the choice from you.
The road is long and the hour is late, and I have no quarrel with you yet. What business brings you across our path?
I do not know your banner, ser {player}, and I prefer it that way until I have reason to learn more. Name yourself and your errand.
Ride on if your road lies elsewhere. My company wishes no news of strangers, and we have no wish to become news ourselves.
Word travels across these hills faster than any herald. I will wait and see whether your tales are true before I trust a single one.
We are {my_faction}, bound by our own oaths and not yet by yours, ser {player}. Keep your hands where I can see them and we shall get on well enough.
A fair day for a meeting, though the weather makes no promises. Tell me what you seek, and I will tell you whether it is mine to give.
Our wagons are heavy and our patience is light. If you mean to trade, speak plainly, ser {player}; if not, the ford lies just behind you.
Many travellers pass this bend and most are forgotten by nightfall. I shall reserve my judgement of you until the sun goes down.
I have no grudge against you, ser {player}, nor any particular fondness. The miles ahead will show which of those we are to share.
Speak your name and your purpose, and I will weigh them on my own scales. The old hills have taught us to be careful with strangers.
Ser {player}, what a sight for weary eyes! Dismount and share our fire, for the road has been cruel and the company is kind.
I had hoped our paths would cross again, friend. My men spoke well of your courage, and now I see for myself that they did not exaggerate.
May the old oaths of the high road keep your horse sure-footed, ser {player}, and your purse heavier than when you rode out.
Few travellers are worth a second greeting, but you, ser {player}, have earned one. Tell me what troubles you, and I will lend my arm to it.
Our house owes a debt to yours, though the ledger has grown musty with age. Consider this meeting the first page of settling it.
Ah, {player}! Your name is spoken with respect at my hearth. Tell me the tale of your latest deeds, and I shall tell you mine.
When the wolves came down from the ridge, you stood firm beside us. That is not a deed a banner forgets, ser {player}.
Ride with us a while, friend. The evening is cold and the road is long, and I would rather have your steel beside me than against me.
I give you my hand and my word, ser {player}. Whatever the next winter brings, my banner will stand with yours.
Ha! Here is a face I did not expect and am glad to see. Come, the wine is poured and our tales are not yet told.
